opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest way to draw the line is to ask what the data is ultimately for, and what it has to be faithful to.

Most of the synthetic data people talk about today, especially in the large language model world, is synthetic data about *information*. You have a model generate text, reasoning traces, question-answer pairs, code. What it needs to be faithful to is human knowledge and logic. If the reasoning is coherent and the answer is correct, the data is useful. Nobody checks whether it obeys gravity.

In autonomous driving and embodied intelligence, the synthetic data is about the *physical world*. What we generate has to stand in for real sensor inputs, camera images, lidar point clouds, IMU readings, tactile signals, and for the consequences of actions. If a robot arm pushes a cup, the cup has to slide, tip, or resist the way a real cup would. If a car brakes on a wet road, the dynamics have to be right. So the bar isn't "does it look plausible to a human" but "does it obey physics closely enough that a policy trained on it still works in reality." That's the sim-to-real gap, and it's the central problem in our field. Text-based synthetic data barely has an equivalent.

A second difference is that our data is closed-loop and interactive. A language model's training data is mostly a static corpus. An embodied agent's data depends on its own behavior: what it sees next depends on what it just did. So in many cases you aren't really generating a dataset, you're generating an *environment*, a world the agent can act in, fail in, and learn from. That makes it closer to building a simulator or world model than to data augmentation.

Third, the value is concentrated in the long tail. For driving, ordinary highway cruising is cheap to collect for real; you have millions of hours of it. What you can't collect safely or economically are the rare, dangerous cases: a child running out from behind a bus, a mattress falling off a truck at night in the rain. Synthetic data is valuable mainly because it can produce those corner cases on demand and in controllable variations. For robotics, the motivation is even stronger, because real robot data is extremely scarce and expensive. You can't scrape it from the internet the way you scrape text.

So I usually summarize it like this: synthetic data for language models mainly scales knowledge and reasoning, while synthetic data for driving and embodied intelligence has to reconstruct the physical world, with correct geometry, appearance, physics, and causality, so an agent can actually act in it. Physical fidelity, interactivity, and coverage of the long tail are what make it a different problem, and frankly a much harder one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical-world sensor data, actions, and interactive environments, but does not identify the data as typically 3D data containing robot trajectories.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good place to start, because I think the term "synthetic data" gets used very loosely, and it hides a real difference in kind.

When people in the language model world say synthetic data, they usually mean one model generating text that another model trains on. The generator and the consumer live in the same medium. You can check the output by reading it, you can filter it with a reward model, and if it's slightly wrong, the cost is a slightly worse answer somewhere down the line. The data describes the world, but it never has to obey the world.

In autonomous driving and embodied intelligence, the data has to obey physics. A synthetic driving scene is not just an image that looks plausible. It encodes the position of every agent, the geometry of the road, the timing of a pedestrian stepping out, the friction on a wet surface. The vehicle takes an action, and the environment has to respond consistently to that action. So what we are really generating is not samples, it's a world the policy can act inside. That closed loop is the first big distinction. Text data is open loop. Embodied data is interactive.

The second distinction is where the ground truth comes from. In the text domain, you often cannot verify whether a synthetic statement is correct without another model or a human judging it. In a simulator, the labels are free and exact. Every bounding box, every depth value, every trajectory is known because the engine put it there. That sounds like a pure advantage, and in one sense it is, but it creates the central problem of our field, which is the sim-to-real gap. The labels are perfect, the pixels and the dynamics are not. A language model doesn't have a rendering gap. We do. A huge amount of the engineering effort goes into making the sensor noise, the lighting, the motor response, the contact physics close enough that what the model learns transfers to a real car or a real robot arm.

The third thing I'd point to is what the data is for. Text synthetic data is mostly about coverage of knowledge and reasoning patterns. Ours is overwhelmingly about the long tail. A fleet of cars will drive millions of kilometers and almost never see a child chasing a ball from behind a bus at dusk in the rain. But that is exactly the case that matters. So we don't generate synthetic data to get more of the average. We generate it to get the rare, dangerous, and expensive-to-collect events, and we need to be able to vary them systematically. Change the weather, change the speed, change the occlusion, and see where the policy breaks.

And one more, which I think is underappreciated. In embodied intelligence the body is part of the data. A dataset collected on one robot with one gripper and one camera mount does not transfer cleanly to another. So synthetic data has to carry the embodiment with it, the kinematics, the sensor placement, the actuator limits. Language has no body. We can't ignore ours.

So if I compress it: text synthetic data is content that a model consumes. Our synthetic data is an environment that an agent inhabits, with exact labels but imperfect fidelity, built mostly to cover what the real world refuses to show us often enough.

r001.rationale: The response mentions scene geometry, agent positions, and trajectories, but it does not clearly identify the synthetic data as typically 3D data containing robot trajectories.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish them by what the data has to represent and what it’s used to train. Synthetic data is a broad category: you might generate text, images, or structured records. In autonomous driving and embodied intelligence, you’re usually trying to represent an agent interacting with a physical world.

That introduces a few requirements. First, physical consistency. A scene can look convincing and still be wrong for training a robot—for example, if objects move unrealistically or contact between objects behaves incorrectly. Second, temporal and sensor consistency. A driving system may use several cameras alongside other sensors, and those observations need to agree with one another and remain coherent over time.

Then there’s the action–consequence relationship. If the agent brakes, turns, or reaches for an object, what happens next? For training and evaluating behavior, generating observations alone isn’t enough; you need the world to respond meaningfully to the agent’s actions.

There are simpler cases, too. Synthetic images can train a perception model without simulating an entire interactive world. So I wouldn’t draw an absolute boundary. The key distinction is how much physical interaction the task requires.

Ultimately, the test is whether the data improves performance in the real world. Visual realism helps, but accurate geometry, useful coverage of difficult situations, and believable responses to actions can matter much more.

r001.rationale: The response describes physical interaction and action consequences, but it does not identify the data as typically 3D or say it contains robot trajectories.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is that, in autonomous driving and embodied intelligence, synthetic data has to represent interaction with the physical world. It’s not enough to generate an image that looks realistic. You need the geometry, motion, and consequences of actions to be consistent.

For example, you can generate a convincing image of a pedestrian crossing a road. But for autonomous driving, you also need to know where that pedestrian is in three dimensions, how they’re moving, what the sensors can observe, and what happens as the car brakes or turns. The data needs to stay consistent over time and across different sensors.

Embodied intelligence adds another layer: the agent changes its environment. If a robot pushes a cup, the cup has to respond in a physically plausible way. So you’re generating not just observations, but a relationship between observations, actions, and outcomes.

That also changes how we judge quality. Visual realism matters, but the more important question is whether training on that synthetic data improves performance in the real world. A beautiful simulation can still teach the wrong behavior, while a simpler simulation can be useful if it captures the factors that matter for the task.

r001.rationale: The response mentions 3D position and action-related motion, but does not identify the data as typically containing robot trajectories.
